Odin in Godot

5 · The two timelines

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Why remote motion renders behindScheduling spatial effectsPresentation timing by causeHolding state for delayed observersPresentation callbacks

In a cooperative game, a gem can disappear before a remote ball visibly reaches it, or remain visible after the local player's ball has passed it.

Replicated state can be correct while presentation looks wrong to observers: the gem vanishes while the rolling ball is still visibly half a meter away, or lingers after the ball has visibly rolled through it.

Local prediction and remote interpolation display different moments. Schedule a spatial effect on the same timeline as its visible cause.

Why remote motion renders behind#

Owner-streamed motion (post 3) is rendered by everyone else through a short interpolation buffer containing a few ticks of samples. This absorbs some jitter and packet loss. A remote ball you're watching is rendered ~100ms behind where its owner's machine says it is. Call these the two timelines:

  • State time is for replicated fields, which arrive as fast as the wire allows. The gem's taken byte flips now.
  • Render time is where remote motion is drawn, at interp-delay in the past. The ball reaches the gem on your screen 100ms from now.

That explains the symptom. The gem's disappearance was keyed to state time; the cause you can see (the ball rolling into it) plays out in render time. Reacting immediately to the state delta makes the effect precede its visible cause. Changing packet delivery alone does not align those clocks.

The collecting player's screen uses local prediction. It can show the pickup in the frame when the command runs, before the authority result arrives, as described in post 4.

Scheduling spatial effects#

When a state change has a moving visible cause, schedule its effect on that cause's presentation clock. Pass a callback to the session and indicate whether the cause came from local simulation:

Odin
// Schedule from the taken-edge on each peer:
ksess.session_present(&self.ses,
	p.net_id == self.my_claim,   // local simulation caused the pickup
	self, present_gem_gone, p.net_id, u64(p.kind))

For a local cause, the callback runs this frame. Otherwise, the session queues it for interp_delay from now to align with the delayed owner stream. Both paths call present_gem_gone, so the presentation procedure can show the same effect without choosing the clock itself. This helper assumes the remote cause is rendered through Kit's interpolated stream; a game-rendered cause must use its own clock, as explained in kit/net.

Hiding the gem in a field setter ties presentation to packet arrival. Keep the state update immediate and schedule the visible disappearance separately.

Presentation timing by cause#

Use the cause to choose which effects need delayed presentation. The full reference is in kit/net:

The consequence of… …presents
my own simulation / my prediction now, with local input
a remote moving cause (ball hits gem, avatar steps on plate) at render time (session_present)
no spatial cause at all (score, hp bar, chat, UI) when the authoritative update arrives
a per-peer local flourish (muzzle flash, footsteps) from local fx hooks (it never rode the wire at all)
a global transition (level change, round end) after a dwell (see below)

A scoreboard has no spatial cause to align with a moving object, so update it when state arrives. Reserve the render delay for effects that need that spatial alignment.

Holding state for delayed observers#

When the ball drops in the cup, puttputt holds the sunk ball there for a couple of seconds before building the next hole:

Odin
SINK_DWELL :: 2.5

Remote screens display the roll up to interp-delay late. If the host advanced the hole as soon as its ball sank, an observer could see the world change while the displayed ball was still approaching the cup. Hold the completed state long enough for the most delayed observer to display it before moving to the next hole.

Deltas send the value present at a network tick. A flag turned on and off within that tick may equal its shadow when compared, so no change is sent. Retain the changed value long enough for replication and presentation, or send a momentary occurrence as an explicit message.

Presentation callbacks#

Presentation code belongs in the presentation proc, never in a command proc. Commands run on the claimer and the host (post 4), so an effect spawned inside a command proc (say, a pickup particle burst inside the powerup_claim command proc) never reaches observers at all, and reconciliation re-runs can spawn it twice.

Spawn the burst inside present_gem_gone. React to the replicated pickup state and schedule that callback for the appropriate display time. Field edges report the net change per frame; if individual occurrences or their counts matter, use a declared presentation event. Keep particles, sounds, and other visible consequences in the presentation callback.

The first three pieces now fit together: replicated state (post 3), predicted commands (post 4), and effects scheduled for each screen's presentation clock. The next post adds persistent identity, recovery, and deployment checks.
